docs.title: Downloading HLS Streams with DevTools and ffmpeg
docs.text: How to download HLS streams with DevTools and ffmpeg on a Windows device.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Website HTML pages used to reference the video source file directly, e.g. src="/media/videos/hello-world.mp4"
  • That means when users load the video source file, they are loading the hello-world.mp4.
  • If the connection is slower than the file's bitrate, playback stalls while it catches up.
  • To improve streaming, the MP4 is broken down into pieces, and each piece is sent one at a time.
  • One of the most widely adopted methods of doing this is HLS (HTTP Live Streaming).

docs.title: HLS Streams
docs.text:
It was originally developed by Apple for iOS/Safari, and it is now supported almost everywhere.

Core structure:

master.m3u8              -> top-level manifest listing the available qualities
  ├── index-1080p.m3u8   -> variant playlist: segment list for one quality
  ├── index-720p.m3u8
  └── index-480p.m3u8

An example master.m3u8:

#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:PROGRAM-ID=1,BANDWIDTH=6126617,RESOLUTION=1996x1080,FRAME-RATE=23.974,CODECS="avc1.64002a,mp4a.40.2"
media-id/1/index-s1080p.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:PROGRAM-ID=1,BANDWIDTH=16160812,RESOLUTION=3840x2076,FRAME-RATE=23.974,CODECS="avc1.640033,mp4a.40.2"
media-id/1/index-s2160p.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:PROGRAM-ID=1,BANDWIDTH=1306696,RESOLUTION=852x480,FRAME-RATE=23.974,CODECS="avc1.4d401e,mp4a.40.2"
media-id/1/index-s480p.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:PROGRAM-ID=1,BANDWIDTH=3140557,RESOLUTION=1332x720,FRAME-RATE=23.974,CODECS="avc1.4d4020,mp4a.40.2"
media-id/1/index-s720p.m3u8

Each variant playlist lists the segments. Traditionally these are .ts files; modern HLS also uses fMP4 .m4s fragments. The playlist carries an #EXT-X-MAP tag for the init segment reference and an #EXTINF tag for each duration:

#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-TARGETDURATION:6
#EXT-X-ALLOW-CACHE:YES
#EXT-X-PLAYLIST-TYPE:VOD
#EXT-X-VERSION:6
#EXT-X-MEDIA-SEQUENCE:1
#EXT-X-MAP:URI="https://example.com/init-s1080p.mp4"

#EXTINF:6.006,
https://example.com/seg-1-s1080p.m4s
#EXTINF:6.006,
https://example.com/seg-2-s1080p.m4s
#EXTINF:6.006,
https://example.com/seg-3-s1080p.m4s
#EXTINF:6.006,
https://example.com/seg-4-s1080p.m4s
#EXTINF:6.006,
https://example.com/seg-5-s1080p.m4s
#EXT-X-ENDLIST

Key characteristics:

  • Plain-text .m3u8 playlists (derived from the M3U audio playlist format)
  • Historically used MPEG-TS segments (.ts); modern HLS supports fMP4 (.m4s) too
  • Native playback support in Safari/iOS (no JS library needed) — this is why it's still dominant in Apple's ecosystem
  • Everywhere else (Chrome, Firefox, Android), it needs a JS library such as hls.js, which uses MSE. This is why you see it under Fetch/XHR
  • Live streaming: the playlist gets new #EXTINF lines appended as segments are encoded, with no #EXT-X-ENDLIST until the stream ends
  • VOD: the playlist is complete upfront and ends with #EXT-X-ENDLIST

Reference: Disable Abusive Debugger Statements

  1. Before going to the target website, visit a site that lets you open the F12 developer tools.
  2. Press F12 to bring up the Developer Tools.
  3. Proceed to the target website.
  4. The developer tools will stop at the "Sources" tab and show the "debugger" line.

  6. Choose the option "Add conditional breakpoint…".

docs.title: Getting the *index*.m3u8 Link
docs.text: There are multiple ways to get the *index*.m3u8 link, i.e. the link that shows the details of the segmented video files. The master playlist, which lists the resolutions of the videos, does not always exist.

docs.title: 1. Search for m3u8
docs.text:
1. From the developer tools (F12), go to the Network tab and search using the keyword m3u8.
  2. There should be a link whose URL ends with m3u8.
  3. Select the link matching *index*.m3u8 and copy its URL.

docs.title: 2. Filter by "Fetch/XHR"
docs.text:
1. From the developer tools (F12), go to the Network tab.
  2. Click the "Fetch/XHR" filter.

  3. You will see a single .m3u8 file, a .mp4 file, and a couple of .m4s files.

  4. Select the link matching *index*.m3u8 and copy its URL.

docs.title: 3. Observe the Network
docs.text:
Info

Method 1 relies on the request name containing m3u8. Method 2 will usually surface the request, but you still have to recognise it by name. Reading the response body works either way.

  1. Open the developer tools (F12) and go to the Network tab.
  2. Refresh the page so that we can see the new links as they come in.
  3. If there is no .m3u8 link, click on each link and read the Response tab.
  4. The response should show plain text with #EXTM3U as the first line (as shown earlier).
  5. Select the link matching *index*.m3u8 and copy its URL.

docs.title: Getting the Media
docs.text:
There are two ways I have tried to download the media.

  1. Use ffmpeg to download the media file.

    ffmpeg -i https://example.com/media-id/1/index-s1080p.m3u8 -c copy saveasvid.mp4

    Info

    Some sites reject ffmpeg because its request headers do not look like a browser's. Copy the headers from the Network tab and pass them in (PowerShell):

    ffmpeg -headers "Referer: https://example.com/`r`nUser-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64)`r`nCookie: session=abc123`r`n" -i "https://example.com/media-id/1/index-s1080p.m3u8" -c copy saveasvid.mp4

    I have not needed this myself, so treat it as untested. It also will not help if the token is only on the .m3u8 URL, because ffmpeg does not add it to the segment requests.

  2. Create a script to download each segment (*.m4s, *.ts, and others such as *.png and *.html), including the *init*.mp4, which stores the information about the media file. Then create a second script that combines the segments and uses ffmpeg to produce a finished .mp4. The following snippet stitches the segments together, in order, into a temporary temp_output.mp4, then calls ffmpeg to create the final combined.mp4.

    """
The snippet only works if the downloaded segments are named
- `init.mp4`
- `seg-*.m4s`
Standardising them helps ensure the script works consistently.
"""
import sys
import pathlib
import shutil
import re
import subprocess

# sort the files by segment number
def _seg_key(p: pathlib.Path) -> int:
    """helper function to sort the file names by the numbers in the segment files"""
    m: re.Match = re.search(r'seg-(\d+)', p.name)
    return int(m.group(1)) if m else -1 # init.mp4 -> -1, so first

# define the temporary folder that holds all the segment files
temp_dir: pathlib.Path = pathlib.Path(__file__).parent / "temp"

# define the temporary .mp4 file after stitching each segment
temp_output_path: pathlib.Path = pathlib.Path(__file__).parent / "temp_output.mp4"

# write each file to the 'temp_output.mp4' file
with temp_output_path.open("wb") as writer:
    for file in sorted(temp_dir.glob("*.*"), key=_seg_key):
        with file.open("rb") as f:
            shutil.copyfileobj(f, writer, length=1024*1024)

# run the ffmpeg command here
try:
    output_name: str = str(pathlib.Path(__file__).parent / "combined.mp4")
    # ffmpeg must be reachable from the terminal
    subprocess.run(
        args=["ffmpeg", "-y", "-i", str(temp_output_path), "-c", "copy", output_name],
        capture_output=False,
        text=False, # set text=True to get stdout/stderr as strings
        check=True, # raises an exception if the exe returns a non-zero exit code
    )
except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e:
    print(f"ffmpeg failed with code {e.returncode}: {e}")
    sys.exit(1)
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("ffmpeg not found on PATH")
    sys.exit(1)

docs.title: Basic Git Problems and Solutions
docs.text: I'm writing the Git problems that I faced here in this blog post. I delve deeper into what the issue is about and how the issue happens. I also present the solutions to the issue, mainly from online.

docs.title: Issue: SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate.
docs.text: This issue usually happens when I'm trying to clone a repository via HTTPS from my work laptop. The error occurs because Git cannot verify the certificate chain due to missing certificates or misconfiguration.

docs.title: The Issue
docs.text:
Two problems can cause this:

Problem 1: Git's CA bundle path is broken

  • Git cannot find its default certificate bundle
  • Check with: git config --get http.sslCAInfo (if it returns empty, this is the problem)

Problem 2: Corporate proxy interference

  • Company proxy intercepts the connection
  • May strip intermediate CA certificates from the chain
  • Or performs SSL inspection, replacing GitHub's cert with company-signed cert
my Git client
> sends 'hello' message

company proxy
> directs the 'hello' message from Git client to GitHub server

the GitHub server
> receives 'hello' message from company proxy
> sends 'hello' message to company proxy
> (containing the github.com cert + intermediate CA cert)

company proxy
> receives the 'hello' message from the server
> strips/blocks the intermediate CA cert
> redirects the 'hello' message from GitHub server to Git client
> intermediate CA lost

my Git client
> receives the 'hello' message
> gets the SSL certificate from the 'hello' message
> verify the SSL certificate with the Certificate Authority (CA)
> unable to verify because missing intermediate CA (incomplete chain)
> presents the error: "unable to get local issuer certificate"

Note: Some corporate proxies also perform SSL inspection, replacing GitHub's certificate entirely with one signed by the company CA. In that case, you'd need to install the company's root CA certificate instead.

docs.title: The Solution
docs.text:
Read some of the solutions here: Stack Overflow

Option 1: Fix Git's CA bundle path (recommended)

# use OpenSSL as the SSL Backend
git config --global http.sslBackend "openssl"

# point Git to its bundled certificates
git config --global http.sslCAInfo "C:\Program Files\Git\mingw64\etc\ssl\certs\ca-bundle.crt"

Option 2: Export and use GitHub's certificate

If option 1 does not work due to the ca-bundle.crt file not present or the ca-bundle certificate is incomplete, try the second option.

  1. Go to the browser and visit the github repository

  2. Click on the lock icon

  3. Get the certificate details (usually there's a certificate icon like the following image)

  4. Export the certificate (or generally export the Root )

  5. Save the exported certificate (file extension can be .cer or .crt - doesn't matter)

  6. Configure Git:

    # Check current setting (if empty, Git can't find CA bundle)
git config --get http.sslCAInfo

# Set to your exported certificate
git config --global http.sslCAInfo "C:\Users\Public\Downloads\github.com.cer"

  7. Retry cloning the repository

docs.title: Graphs Basics Part I: Representation
docs.text:
Before we can run BFS, DFS, or Dijkstra, we need a way to actually store a graph. This part covers the three standard representations — adjacency matrix, adjacency list, and edge list — with Python code and a cheat sheet for picking between them.

A graph \(G = (V, E)\) is a set of vertices (nodes) \(V\) together with a set of edges \(E\), where each edge connects a pair of vertices. Examples of how graphs can be used in our daily lives: a road map (intersections are vertices, roads are edges), a social network (people, follow relationships), a build system (tasks, dependency order).

On the other hand, a tree is a graph — specifically a connected graph with no cycles. Trees have a root and a parent-before-child hierarchy; general graphs have neither, which means an edge can point "backwards," a vertex can have many neighbours with no hierarchy between them, and you can walk in circles, so traversal algorithms need a visited set.

This post assumes undirected, unweighted graphs — directed edges and weights change the picture and are out of scope here.

docs.title: Representations
docs.text:
There are 3 ways to represent a graph:

  1. Adjacency Matrix (2D Matrix)
  2. Adjacency List
  3. Edge List

Our running example throughout this post will be a 4-cycle:

0 - 1
|   |
2 - 3

The four edges are \((0,1), (0,2), (1,3), (2,3)\): keep that list in mind, it appears in every code sample. In the following examples, each vertex in the graph is represented as an integer.

docs.title: 1. Adjacency Matrix
docs.text:
• a 2D matrix: Edge \((i,j)\) is stored at matrix[i][j] (and matrix[j][i] since the graph is undirected); the cell is 1 if the edge exists, 0 otherwise.
Details Advantages
  • \(O(1)\) edge lookup
  • very simple
  • great for dense graphs — when \(E \approx V^2\) the matrix wastes almost nothing and its \(O(1)\) lookup beats the list's \(O(\deg(u))\)
Disadvantages
  • \(O(V^{2})\) memory: unusable for \(\lvert V \rvert = 10^{5}\)
  • getting the neighbours requires \(O(V)\)
  • An example representation in Python code would be:
# define the number of vertices
V: int = 4

# adjacency matrix is a 2D matrix of size |V| * |V|
matrix: list[list[int]] = [[0] * V for _ in range(V)]

# define the function to add edge in the graph
def add_edge(matrix: list[list[int]], u: int, v: int) -> None:
    matrix[u][v] = 1
    matrix[v][u] = 1

# define the edges list
edges: list[tuple[int, int]] = [(0,1), (0,2), (1,3), (2,3)]

# add the edges for the graph
for u, v in edges:
    add_edge(matrix, u, v)
  • After running, the structure is:
matrix: list[list[int]] = [
# vertex 0, 1, 2, 3
       [ 0, 1, 1, 0 ], # vertex 0
       [ 1, 0, 0, 1 ], # vertex 1
       [ 1, 0, 0, 1 ], # vertex 2
       [ 0, 1, 1, 0 ], # vertex 3
]
  • Notice that the matrix is symmetric along the diagonal axis because the graph is undirected.

  • If the value in matrix[i][j] where i = j is equal to 1, then there is a self-loop within the vertex.

  • Common operations:

# getting the neighbours of u
def neighbours(matrix: list[list[int]], u: int) -> list[int]:
    return [v for v in range(len(matrix)) if matrix[u][v]]

# edge check: does vertex u and v have an edge
def has_edge(matrix: list[list[int]], u: int, v: int) -> bool:
    return matrix[u][v] != 0

docs.title: 2. Adjacency List
docs.text:
• The default choice — \(O(V+E)\) memory handles the sparse graphs real problems have.
  • The list at index \(u\) stores all of \(u\)'s neighbours.
Details Advantages
  • \(O(V + E)\) memory
  • \(O(\deg(u))\) neighbour iteration
Disadvantages
  • \(O(\deg(u))\) edge lookup
  • An example representation in Python code would be:
# define the number of vertices in the graph
V: int = 4

# define the adjacency list
adjacency_list: list[list[int]] = [[] for _ in range(V)]

# define the function to add edge in the graph
def add_edge(adjacency_list: list[list[int]], u: int, v: int):
    adjacency_list[u].append(v)
    adjacency_list[v].append(u)

# define the edges list
edges: list[tuple[int, int]] = [(0,1), (0,2), (1,3), (2,3)]

# add each edge to the adjacency list
for u, v in edges:
    add_edge(adjacency_list, u, v)
  • After running, the structure is:
adjacency_list: list[list[int]] = [
    [ 1, 2 ], # vertex 0
    [ 0, 3 ], # vertex 1
    [ 0, 3 ], # vertex 2
    [ 1, 2 ], # vertex 3
]
  • Notice that adjacency_list[0] = [1, 2] is exactly the 1-positions of row 0 of the adjacency matrix.

  • Note: Storing each neighbour list as a set instead of a list turns the \(O(\deg(u))\) edge lookup into expected \(O(1)\), at a slightly higher memory cost. It's the single most common practical upgrade.

  • Common operations:

# getting the neighbours of u
def neighbours(adjacency_list: list[list[int]], u: int) -> list[int]:
    return adjacency_list[u]

# edge check: does vertex u and v have an edge
def has_edge(adjacency_list: list[list[int]], u: int, v: int) -> bool:
    return v in adjacency_list[u]

docs.title: 3. Edge List
docs.text:
• A list in which each tuple \((u, v)\) is a single edge of the graph.
Details Advantages
  • \(O(E)\) memory
  • ideal when the algorithm only needs to iterate all edges once, e.g. Kruskal's, Bellman-Ford, building an adjacency list, DSU-driven problems
Disadvantages
  • neighbours and edge lookup are both \(O(E)\) full scans
  • useless for BFS/DFS/matching directly
  • An example representation in Python code would be:
# define the number of vertices
V: int = 4

# define the edge list
edge_list: list[tuple[int, int]] = [ (0,1), (0,2), (1,3), (2,3) ]
  • Notice that the edge list is exactly the input format most problems give: "the next \(E\) lines each contain two vertices."
  • Nothing is converted or restructured: read the edges and store them as-is, which is why it costs \(O(1)\) to build.

  • That's what makes it ideal for algorithms that sweep every edge exactly once — Kruskal's, Bellman-Ford, DSU (all algorithms that work on weighted graphs which are not discussed in this post) — and for one very common job: turning the raw edges into an adjacency list.

  • Common Operations:

# getting the neighbours of u
def neighbours(edge_list: list[tuple[int, int]], u: int) -> list[int]:
    n: list[int] = []
    for v_u, v_v in edge_list:
        if u == v_u:
            n.append(v_v)
        elif u == v_v:
            n.append(v_u)
    return n

# edge check: does vertex u and v have an edge
def has_edge(edge_list: list[tuple[int, int]], u: int, v: int) -> bool:
    for v_u, v_v in edge_list:
        if ((u == v_u and v == v_v) or (u == v_v and v == v_u)):
            return True
    return False

  • Floyd-Warshall
  • BFS/DFS
  • Matching
  • Most problems
  • Kruskal
  • Bellman-Ford

docs.text: Part I ended with a graph stored in an adjacency list. This part walks it: the two most important traversal algorithms — BFS and DFS — with an interactive animation, the mark-on-push vs mark-on-pop variants, and worked grid examples (reachable region, connected components).

docs.title: BFS/DFS Traversal Algorithms (Iterative)
docs.text:
• The two most important graph traversal algorithms.
  • BFS (or Breadth First Search) visits the adjacent vertices (all the neighbours) first before visiting the other vertices.
  • On the other hand, DFS (or Depth First Search) visits the next vertex recursively before going to the rest of its adjacent vertices (or neighbours).
  • Below is an animation to help visualising BFS/DFS traversal in a graph (Made by Qwen 3.8 Flash Next).

in the frontier (seen, not finished) the vertex being expanded done edge blocked by the visited set

docs.title: Build the Graph
docs.text:
• Before showing the traversal code, with Part I knowledge, let's build the graph in adjacency list first.
  • Below code will store each vertex as a string.
# build the edge_list
edge_list: list[tuple[str, str]] = [
    ("A", "B"), ("A", "C"),
    ("B", "D"), ("B", "E"),
    ("C", "F"), ("C", "G"),
    ("D", "H"), ("E", "H"), ("F", "H"), ("G", "H")
]

# build the adjacency list
vertex_names: list[str] = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G", "H"]
adjacency_list: dict[str, list[str]] = {}
for vertex_name in vertex_names:
    if (adjacency_list.get(vertex_name) is None):
        adjacency_list[vertex_name] = []

# add the edges
for u, v in edge_list:
    adjacency_list.get(u).append(v)
    adjacency_list.get(v).append(u)
  • The code above will output the below.
adjacency_list: dict[str, list[str]] = {
    'A': ['B', 'C'], 
    'B': ['A', 'D', 'E'], 
    'C': ['A', 'F', 'G'], 
    'D': ['B', 'H'], 
    'E': ['B', 'H'], 
    'F': ['C', 'H'], 
    'G': ['C', 'H'], 
    'H': ['D', 'E', 'F', 'G']
}

  • Below table shows the space and time complexity of both DFS and BFS algorithms.

    DFS & BFS Time Complexity \(O(V+E)\) Space Complexity \(O(V)\)

  • Both codes below show the iterative algorithm because some programming languages have a recursion-depth. For example, python -c "import sys; print(sys.getrecursionlimit())" will show the recursion-depth.

docs.title: DFS Algorithm (Iterative)
docs.text:
def dfs(adjacency_list: dict[str, list[str]], start_node: str) -> list[str]:

    # define three variables: stack, visited and the current node
    stack: list[str] = [start_node] # stack is last-in-first-out (LIFO)
    visited: set[str] = {start_node}
    cur_node: str = start_node

    # define the output
    order: list[str] = []

    # iteratively perform the DFS traversal
    while (len(stack) != 0):
        cur_node = stack.pop() # get the current node
        order.append(cur_node)
        for v in adjacency_list.get(cur_node):
            if (v not in visited):
                stack.append(v)
                visited.add(v)

    return order

docs.title: BFS Algorithm (Iterative)
docs.text:
• BFS differs from DFS by using a queue instead of a stack.

  • Use collections.deque to initialise as a queue.

from collections import deque

def bfs(adjacency_list: dict[str, list[str]], start_node: str) -> list[str]:

    # define the three variables: queue, visited and the current node
    queue: deque[str] = deque([start_node]) # queue is first-in-first-out (FIFO)
    visited: set[str] = {start_node}
    cur_node: str = start_node

    # define the output
    order: list[str] = []

    # iteratively perform the BFS traversal
    while (len(queue) != 0):
        cur_node = queue.popleft()
        order.append(cur_node)
        for v in adjacency_list.get(cur_node):
            if (v not in visited):
                queue.append(v)
                visited.add(v)

    return order

Info

The above algorithms are using the "mark-on-push" and "mark-on-enqueue" variants for DFS and BFS respectively. This means that the node is marked as visited after it is pushed/enqueued to the stack/queue (as shown in lines 17 and 18 for DFS and lines 19 and 20 for BFS).

Another variant is the "mark-on-pop" and "mark-on-dequeue" where the node is marked as visited after it is popped/dequeued from the stack/queue. For DFS the visit order can change: on the animated graph starting from A, mark-on-push gives A C G H E D F B while mark-on-pop gives A C G H F E B D. For BFS the visit order never changes between the two variants (A B C D E F G H from A either way) — what changes is only how much the stack/queue swells, as discussed below.

Although both variants work, "mark-on-pop" and "mark-on-dequeue" variants are more inefficient than their counterpart. This is evident when the graph is a complete graph, i.e. each vertex has an edge to every other vertex except itself. This is because the node is only marked visited after it is popped/dequeued. Each neighbour will be added because it has not been visited yet — including neighbours that are already sitting in the stack/queue. Therefore, there will be duplicate nodes in the stack/queue: mark-on-push/mark-on-enqueue enters every vertex at most once (\(O(V)\) pushes/enqueues in total), while mark-on-pop/mark-on-dequeue can reach \(O(E)\). Concretely, on the complete graph \(K_{6}\) a traversal from any start vertex performs exactly 6 pushes/enqueues with mark-on-push/mark-on-enqueue, but 16 with mark-on-pop/mark-on-dequeue — in general, \(n\) versus \(n + \frac{(n-1)(n-2)}{2}\) for \(K_{n}\).

DFS mark on pop variant

def dfs_mark_on_pop(adjacency_list: dict[str, list[str]], start_node: str) -> list[str]:

    # define the three variables: stack, visited and the current node
    stack: list[str] = [start_node]
    cur_node: str = start_node

    # === diff from mark on push variant ===
    visited: set[str] = set()
    # === diff ends ===

    # define the output
    order: list[str] = []

    # iteratively perform the DFS traversal
    while (len(stack) != 0):
        cur_node = stack.pop() # get the current node

        # === here's where it differs from "mark-on-push" ===
        if (cur_node in visited):
            continue
        visited.add(cur_node)
        # === diff end ===

        order.append(cur_node)
        for v in adjacency_list.get(cur_node):
            if (v not in visited):
                stack.append(v)

    return order

BFS mark on dequeue variant

def bfs_mark_on_dequeue(adjacency_list: dict[str, list[str]], start_node: str) -> list[str]:

    # define the three variables: queue, visited and the current node
    queue: deque[str] = deque([start_node])
    cur_node: str = start_node

    # === diff from mark on enqueue variant ===
    visited: set[str] = set()
    # === diff ends ===

    # define the output
    order: list[str] = []

    # iteratively perform the BFS traversal
    while (len(queue) != 0):
        cur_node = queue.popleft() # queue is first-in-first-out (FIFO)

        # === here's where it differs from "mark-on-enqueue" ===
        if (cur_node in visited):
            continue
        visited.add(cur_node)
        # === diff end ===

        order.append(cur_node)
        for v in adjacency_list.get(cur_node):
            if (v not in visited):
                queue.append(v)

    return order

docs.title: Grid Traversal Algorithm
docs.text:
• A grid is an implicit graph.
  • Each cell (row, column) is a vertex.
  • Each of its up/down/left/right/(optionally)diagonals neighbours is an edge. For example, if (0,0) and (0,1) are both . (open cell), then there's an edge from (0,0) to (0,1).
  • "Grid traversal" is essentially a BFS or DFS over the implicit graph.

docs.title: Example Problem
docs.text:
• You're given an R × C grid of characters. '.' is open, '#' is a wall. Given a starting cell (sr, sc) which is guaranteed open, count how many open cells are reachable from it by moving up/down/left/right through open cells.

    row 0:  .  .  #  .  .
row 1:  .  .  #  #  #
row 2:  .  .  #  .  .

  • Start at (0,0), solutions: 6 (the connected open region containing the start).

  • Start at (0,3), solutions: 2.

docs.title: Step 1: Build the Graph (Adjacency List)
docs.text:
def build_graph(grid: list[list[str]]) -> dict[tuple[int, int], set[tuple[int, int]]]:

    # get number of rows and number of columns
    no_of_rows: int = len(grid)
    no_of_cols: int = len(grid[0])

    # each vertex is indicated by its coordinate (row,col)
    adjacency_list: dict[tuple[int, int], set[tuple[int, int]]] = {} # init the adjacency_list
    edge_list: list[tuple[tuple[int, int], tuple[int, int]]] = [] # build the edge list
    for i in range(no_of_rows):
        for j in range(no_of_cols):

            if (grid[i][j] == "#"):
                continue

            # initialise the adjacent vertex list
            adjacency_list[(i,j)] = set()

            # add an edge for "right" direction
            right: int = j + 1
            if (right <= no_of_cols - 1 and grid[i][right] != "#"):
                edge_list.append(((i,j), (i,right)))

            # add an edge for "left" direction
            left: int = j - 1
            if (left >= 0 and grid[i][left] != "#"):
                edge_list.append(((i,j), (i,left)))

            # add an edge for "up" direction
            up: int = i - 1
            if (up >= 0 and grid[up][j] != "#"):
                edge_list.append(((i,j), (up,j)))

            # add an edge for "down" direction
            down: int = i + 1
            if (down <= no_of_rows - 1 and grid[down][j] != "#"):
                edge_list.append(((i,j), (down,j)))

    # add the edge
    for u, v in edge_list:
        adjacency_list[u].add(v)
        adjacency_list[v].add(u)

    return adjacency_list

docs.title: Step 2: Count the Number of Open Cells Using BFS (or DFS if you prefer)
docs.text:
def count_open_cells(adjacency_list: dict[tuple[int, int], set[tuple[int, int]]], start_coor: tuple[int, int]) -> int:

    # initialise the count
    count: int = 0

    # perform the BFS traversal
    queue: deque[tuple[int, int]] = deque([start_coor])
    visited: set[tuple[int, int]] = {start_coor}
    cur_node: tuple[int, int] = start_coor
    while (len(queue) != 0):
        cur_node = queue.popleft()
        count += 1
        for v in adjacency_list.get(cur_node):
            if (v not in visited):
                queue.append(v)
                visited.add(v)

    return count

docs.title: A Shorter Solution: Skip the Graph
docs.text:
• The previous steps show a clearer way to solve the problem. However, building the graph is not needed.
  • The problem can be solved with fewer steps: skipping building the graph directly.
  • A direction array stores the (row, col) offsets of the allowed moves; for diagonals, just add (-1,-1), (-1,1), (1,-1), (1,1) to directions.

  • Every edge in this problem goes from a cell to an adjacent cell, so a neighbour is fully described by:

    1. within bounds (0 <= new_row < no_of_rows and 0 <= new_col < no_of_cols)
    2. not a wall (grid[new_row][new_col] != "#")
    3. and not visited yet

  • That is all BFS needs — no graph required.

def count_open_cells_v2(grid: list[list[str]], start_coor: tuple[int, int]) -> int:

    no_of_rows: int = len(grid)
    no_of_cols: int = len(grid[0])

    # direction array: up, down, left and right respectively
    directions: list[tuple[int, int]] = [(-1,0), (1,0), (0,-1), (0,1)]

    # initialise the count
    count: int = 0

    # perform the BFS traversal directly
    # no need to build the graph
    queue: deque[tuple[int, int]] = deque([start_coor])
    visited: set[tuple[int, int]] = {start_coor}
    cur_node: tuple[int, int] = start_coor
    while (len(queue) != 0):
        cur_node = queue.popleft()
        count += 1
        for d_row, d_col in directions:
            new_row: int = cur_node[0] + d_row
            new_col: int = cur_node[1] + d_col
            if (0 <= new_row < no_of_rows and 0 <= new_col < no_of_cols and grid[new_row][new_col] != "#" and (new_row, new_col) not in visited):
                queue.append((new_row, new_col))
                visited.add((new_row, new_col))

    return count
  • Both solutions end up at \(O(R \cdot C)\) time and \(O(R \cdot C)\) memory in the worst case, so either is fast enough.
  • The real difference is when and where the work happens:
    • Step 1 pays \(O(R \cdot C)\) before the traversal even starts — it inspects every cell of the grid to build the graph, even if the reachable region turns out to be a handful of cells.
    • The direction-array version only ever touches the reachable region itself: each cell is dequeued once and checks its 4 directions, so it is \(O(\text{reachable cells})\).
  • Memory tells the same story: the Step 1 version keeps the whole adjacency list (every open cell and its edges) for the entire traversal, while the direction-array version only keeps visited and the queue.
  • As a rule of thumb: BFS/DFS on an adjacency list costs \(O(V + E)\) — every vertex is dequeued once and every edge is scanned once — and here \(V \le R \cdot C\) and \(E \le 2 \cdot R \cdot C\), which is why both collapse to \(O(R \cdot C)\).

docs.title: Connected Components
docs.text:
• A connected component is a group of cells where every cell can reach every other cell in the same group; cells in different components cannot reach each other — that is what separates them.
  • One BFS/DFS run only ever discovers the start cell's own component.
  • So the pattern is:
    1. run a traversal from a cell
    2. keep a visited set of the cells it found
    3. then start a new traversal from the next cell that is not in visited yet
    4. and repeat until there are no unvisited cells left.

docs.title: Example Problem
docs.text:
• You're given an \(R \times C\) grid of '.' (open) and '#' (wall). Two open cells are in the same component if you can walk between them through open cells using up/down/left/right moves. Return the list of connected components.

  • On the Example Problem's grid, the answer is 3 components:

    • sizes 6, 2 and 2:
      • {(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1),(2,0),(2,1)}
      • {(0,3),(0,4)} and
      • {(2,3),(2,4)}.
    • The order in which the components — and the cells within each — come out depends on dict order and stack order, so compare contents, not positions.

  • Use the build_graph function above to build the graph

  • Below is the code for finding the list of connected components

def get_connected_components(adjacency_list: dict[tuple[int, int], set[tuple[int, int]]]) -> list[list[tuple[int, int]]]:

    # every cell must still be checked once by the loop below, but cells already
    # assigned to a component must not start a second DFS — otherwise the same
    # component is found again (and again)
    visited: set[tuple[int, int]] = set()

    def dfs(adjacency_list: dict[tuple[int, int], set[tuple[int, int]]], start_coor: tuple[int, int]):

        # initialise the variable that stores the cells that are connected in the grid
        connected: list[tuple[int, int]] = []

        # initialise the common variables to perform the DFS traversal
        start_node: tuple[int, int] = start_coor
        stack: list[tuple[int, int]] = [start_node]
        curr_node: tuple[int, int] = start_node

        # visited is already defined above at line 6
        visited.add(start_node)

        # iteratively perform the DFS traversal
        while (len(stack) != 0):
            curr_node = stack.pop()
            connected.append(curr_node)
            for v in adjacency_list.get(curr_node):
                if (v not in visited):
                    stack.append(v)
                    visited.add(v)

        return connected

    output: list[list[tuple[int, int]]] = []
    for u in adjacency_list:
        if u in visited:
            continue
        connected: list[tuple[int, int]] = dfs(adjacency_list, u)
        output.append(connected)

    return output
  • This isn't grid-specific: for any graph, for u in adjacency_list: if u not in visited: dfs(u) is the standard pattern for enumerating components.
  • The same outer loop is exactly what is needed when a traversal must cover a possibly-disconnected graph.
  • Complexity: Every cell is pushed and popped across all the DFS runs combined at most once, so the whole function is \(O(V + E)\) — the same cost as a single traversal.

docs.title: Setting Up PostgreSQL on Windows 11
docs.text: In this blog post, I am documenting the steps that I took to set up PostgreSQL on my local machine (Windows 11).

docs.title: The Steps I Took
docs.text:
1. Link: Download PostgreSQL on Windows
  2. Click on the link "Download the installer certified by EDB for all supported Postgres versions."
  3. Install based on the OS (in my case: Windows 11)
  4. Once the installation has completed, click on the installer
  5. Below are the setup questions
    • Installation Directory: "C:\Program Files\PostgreSQL\18"
    • Additional Components to be installed:
      • PostgreSQL server
      • pgAdmin 4
      • Stack Builder
      • Command Line Tools
    • Data Directory: "C:\Program Files\PostgreSQL\18\data"
    • Provide password for the database superuser (postgres). 'postgres' is the superuser's username
    • Port: 5432
    • Locale (used by the new database cluster): DEFAULT
  6. After the setup has completed, I unchecked the option to launch stack builder at exit
  7. After clicking on the "Finish" button, PostgreSQL server started in the background.
    • To check: open Task Manager and search for postgre
    • There should be 1 background process: PostgreSQL Server
  8. Installation Completed!

docs.title: The Additional Component - pgAdmin 4
docs.text:
Back when I was in university learning SQL, I was confused with the different applications I needed to download to run PostgreSQL. I will try to break down the purposes of different applications in this section.

Firstly, we have PostgreSQL server. This is the database server. It listens to incoming connections and accepts them. It runs the queries that users ask and return the output. The PostgreSQL server is the main component.

Then, we have pgAdmin 4 which is like a graphical user interface to the PostgreSQL server. Opening up pgAdmin 4 for the first time, you will see one server already installed - PostgreSQL 18 (which is the version that was installed). When pgAdmin 4 is first opened, it prompts for the 'postgres' user that was set during installation. Check the "Save Password" for the application to remember.

There should be a default "postgres" database already created for the superuser "postgres". You can create a new database by selecting the "Databases" dropdown, right-click, click on "Create" and "Database...".

On the left-hand side, on the third row, there's a workspace button. The workspace is something like an SSH terminal to connect to a PostgreSQL database server instead of a normal server. Input the following to access the terminal and run SQL queries. Then, click on "Connect & Open PSQL".

Server Name: localhost
Host name/address: 127.0.0.1
Port: 5432
Database: the database
User: postgres
Password: [password]

docs.title: Working with Python SQLAlchemy ORM
docs.text:
The following code shows a simple way of using SQLAlchemy ORM to connect to a PostgreSQL database. If it fails, it will show errors. Ensure that the database is already created.

# pip install psycopg2 (or psycopg2-binary)
from sqlalchemy import create_engine

# this should be in .env (hardcoded for viewing purposes in this blog)
DATABASE_URL="postgresql+psycopg2://username:password@localhost:5432/db_name"

# create database engine
engine = create_engine(DATABASE_URL)

# connect to the PostgreSQL database
try:
    conn = engine.connect()
    print('Connected')

    # close the PostgreSQL database connection
    conn.close()
except Exception as e:
    print(f'Failed to connect: {e}')

docs.title: Shared Project Learnings
docs.text: My friend and I have been working on a website for golfers to input and track their scores on a leaderboard, competing against their friends. We use FastAPI as our backend and PostgreSQL as the primary database. In this blog, I am writing notes and lessons I have taken as we develop the app.

docs.title: Source Control
docs.text:
When starting a new feature in a shared project, it is ideal to create a new branch and work on that branch instead of the main branch. This is to prevent conflicts during development. The typical workflow usually goes like this:

git checkout dev
git pull origin dev # make sure your local dev is up to date first!
git checkout -b feature/feature-A # branch off dev
git push -u origin feature/feature-A # first push, sets upstream tracking

Once the feature feature/feature-A is completed, you can either:

  1. Open a pull request and merge feature/feature-A to the dev branch. OR

  2. Merge locally and then push to the repository.

    git checkout dev
git pull origin dev # get the latest dev
git merge feature/feature-A # merge feature/feature-A to dev branch
git push # push to the repository

Branch names are equally important. Use hyphens rather than underscores. Here is how to name the branch according to the work.

  1. For new functionality or new features, name the branch feature/<feature-name>
  2. For fixing bugs in the code, name the branch bugfix/<bugfix-name>
  3. For urgent production patches, name the branch hotfix/<hotfix-name>
  4. For preparing new releases, name the branch release/<release-version>
  5. For refactoring the code, name the branch refactor/<feature-name>
  6. For updating/writing documentation, name the branch docs/<feature-name>

docs.title: Forgot postgres User Password? Here's the Fix.
docs.text:
I had a problem trying to sign in as the postgres user. I tried different passwords but all of them failed. I had to reset the password and here is what I did.

  1. Locate the pg_hba.conf file: C:\Program Files\PostgreSQL\18\data\pg_hba.conf. It is usually located in the installed folder of PostgreSQL.
  2. Temporarily edit pg_hba.conf to allow trust authentication. In the line for host connections on 127.0.0.1/32, remove the word scram-sha-256 and change it to trust. For e.g. 
    host    all             all             127.0.0.1/32            scram-sha-256
    to 
    host    all             all             127.0.0.1/32            trust
  3. Restart the PostgreSQL service in Windows: open services, look for postgresql-x64-18 - PostgreSQL Server 18 and restart the PostgreSQL service.
  4. Open pgAdmin4 or psql and run the following command: 
    ALTER USER postgres WITH PASSWORD 'new_password';
  5. Restart pgAdmin4 or psql and log in using the new password. It should work. Close the applications.
  6. Edit pg_hba.conf back to the original. From 
    host    all             all             127.0.0.1/32            trust
    to 
    host    all             all             127.0.0.1/32            scram-sha-256
  7. Restart the PostgreSQL service, similar to step 3.

docs.title: Software Development Tips
docs.text:
The first not-so-obvious mistake when I was developing the FastAPI backend was writing everything in the router layer (database queries, business logic, etc.). That is not the ideal way as it increases the difficulty to test the code. It is fine for small projects, but it is better to separate them into different layers. Here is what I initially did:

backend/
├─ app/
│  ├ core/
│  │  ├ __init__.py
│  │  ├ config.py
│  │  └ database.py    # init database engine and session
│  ├ models/
│  │  ├ __init__.py
│  │  ├ base.py
│  │  └ courses.py     # the SQLAlchemy model
│  ├ routers/
│  │  ├ __init__.py
│  │  └ course.py      # the FastAPI router
│  ├ schemas/
│  │  ├ __init__.py
│  │  └ course.py      # the Pydantic model
│  ├ __init__.py
│  ├ main.py
├─ tests/
│  ├ __init__.py
│  ├ conftest.py
│  └ test_golf_course.py

The business logic and the database queries all end up in a single course.py in the routers folder. The general advice with HTTP routers is that they need to be as lightweight as possible. The routers usually just return whatever the service layer is providing. The service layer should only handle the business logic. Therefore, this also requires a database (or a client) layer to fetch the data. Below is a more ideal version.

backend/
├─ app/
│  ├ core/
│  │  ├ __init__.py
│  │  ├ config.py
│  │  └ database.py    # init database engine and session
│  ├ models/           # define the SQLAlchemy models
│  │  ├ __init__.py
│  │  ├ base.py
│  │  └ courses.py
│  ├ clients/          # the client layer - fetches data
│  │  ├ __init__.py
│  │  └ course.py
│  ├ schemas/          # define the Pydantic models - type checking
│  │  ├ __init__.py
│  │  └ course.py
│  ├ services/         # the service layer - business logic
│  │  ├ __init__.py
│  │  └ course.py
│  ├ routers/          # the FastAPI HTTP router
│  │  ├ __init__.py
│  │  └ course.py
│  ├ __init__.py
│  ├ main.py
├─ tests/
│  ├ __init__.py
│  ├ conftest.py
│  └ test_golf_course.py

docs.title: Understanding SSL/TLS Handshake
docs.text: I explain how SSL/TLS handshake works in an easy-to-understand manner in this blog post. I went a bit deeper on this topic because I thought one of the git problems that I faced was related to SSL/TLS handshake (You can read that here - Issue: SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate).

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
I mainly learned how it works from these links:

  • How does SSL work?
  • What Happens in a TLS Handshake?

I find it easier if I can lay the details down in a simplified format.

docs.title: SSL/TLS Handshake
docs.text:
Below is the flow of TLS handshake using the RSA key exchange algorithm. However, the TLS handshake using the RSA key exchange algorithm is now considered not secure. The TLS handshake that uses RSA key exchange algorithm or other cipher suites that are vulnerable to attacks is now being replaced by TLS 1.3. Before going to TLS 1.3, I will explain the SSL/TLS handshake first.

There are two entities that are involved in a TLS handshake.

  • client: the user that visits a domain
  • server: the entity that handles/serves the client

A TLS handshake is necessary before any communication happens between the client and server to ensure that both parties are genuine. Clients do not want to talk to a server that can harm them. The communication is similar to how two people text.

docs.title: Part I: Ensuring Server is Genuine
docs.text:
In the first part of the communication, the client will try to verify that the server is genuine and safe before continuing with the rest of the communications. The client will request for SSL certificates that are compared against the Certificate Authority (CA). CA will check with its database and return whether the server is genuine.

client: "hello"
client: "here is a list of TLS version I support"
client: "here is a list of cipher suites I support"
client: "here is the random bytes I generate (also
         known as the 'client random')"

server: "hello"
server: "here is my SSL certificate. you can extract
         my public key inside"
server: "let's use this TLS version 'x.x'"
server: "let's use this 'xxx' cipher suite"
server: "here is the random bytes I generate (also
         known as the 'server random')"

client: "I have received your SSL certificate. I
         will now verify it with the certificate
         authority (CA) that issued your certificate."

client: ...opens local trust store...
client: ...uses CA's public key to verify the certificate's
           signature locally...

client: "I have verified and concluded you are not
         fake. We can continue our communication."

docs.title: Part II: Generate Session Keys
docs.text:
Once the client knows that the server is genuine, both the server and the client will generate the exact same session keys to communicate over the network. The communication will be encrypted with the session keys to ensure privacy.

client: ...generate another random string of bytes (
           also known as 'premaster secret')...
client: ...encrypt the 'premaster secret' with server's
           public key...

client: "Here is the premaster secret"
client: "I have encrypted it (the premaster secret) with
         your public key"

server: "I have received your premaster secret. I will
         now decrypt it using my private key"
server: "Now I'll generate session keys using your 'client
         random', your 'premaster secret' and my 'server
         random'"

client: "I have also generated session keys using my
         'client random', your 'server random' and my 
         'premaster secret'"
client: "I will encrypt my message 'finished' with the
         session keys"
client: "Here is my encrypted 'finished' message"

server: "I will decrypt your 'finished' message with my
         session keys"
server: "It says 'finished'. Our session keys match!"
server: "I will now encrypt my message 'finished'
         with our session keys"
server: "Here is my encrypted 'finished' message"

client: "I decrypted your 'finished' successfully!"
client: "We're synchronized and secure!"

The "finished" messages are the proof of matching keys, not a transmission of the keys themselves.

docs.title: Vulnerability with SSL/TLS Handshake
docs.text:
One of the ways to attack is via the Poodle Attack SSL which was discovered by Google security researches Bodo Möller, Thai Duong, and Krzysztof Kotowicz. Learn more about POODLE attack here - What is Poodle Attack SSL. The below shows how the attacker forces the client and the server to communicate using an unsafe SSL protocol.

client: "hello, I support TLS 1.2, 1.1, 1.0, SSL 3.0"

attacker: ...deliberately DISRUPTS/DROPS the handshake packets...
          ...causes a connection failure...

client: "let me retry with a lower version..."
client: "hello, I support TLS 1.1, 1.0, SSL 3.0"

attacker: ...disrupts again...

client: "let me retry again..."
client: "hello, I support TLS 1.0, SSL 3.0"

attacker: ...disrupts again...

client: "last resort..."
client: "hello, I support SSL 3.0 only"

server: "okay, SSL 3.0 it is!"

attacker: "perfect, now I can exploit CBC padding!"

Now both the server and the client are connected with SSL 3.0 that the attacker can attack easily. I'm not going to explain how SSL 3.0 can be attacked. It is above my pay grade. Essentially, the attacker will modify the encrypted message of the client. The server will respond with 'valid padding' or 'invalid padding'. The attacker will mathematically determine the plaintext data one byte at a time based on the server's response and the modified ciphertext. The response by the server is the 'oracle'. Hence, the name of this attack is called POODLE (Padding Oracle On Downgraded Legacy Encryption). The attacker does not need to know the session keys.

docs.title: Solution: Handshake in TLS 1.3
docs.text:
The simplified version (also as explained in What Happens in a TLS Handshake?) of the handshake in TLS 1.3 is as below.

Client sends 'hello' message with

  • the protocol version
  • the client random
  • a list of cipher suites.
  • premaster secret parameters (the ingredients to calculate the premaster secret)

The client assumes that it knows the server's preferred key exchange method due to the limited number of cipher suites in TLS 1.3. This also speeds up the handshake in TLS 1.3.

After receiving the 'hello' message from the client, the server generates the master secret from

  • the client random
  • the client's premaster secret parameters
  • the cipher suite chosen
  • the server random

The server then sends the 'hello' message which includes

  • the server's certificate
  • the digital signature
  • the server random
  • the chosen cipher suite

Since the server already has the master secret, it also sends the 'finished' message.

The client then verifies signature and certificate. It also generates the master secret and sends its 'finished' message to the server.

TLS 1.3 includes performance improvements like 0-RTT (Zero Round-Trip Time), which reduces round trips for returning users. TLS 1.3 prevents the POODLE Attack SSL by completely rejecting SSL 3.0 and removing vulnerable CBC cipher suites entirely.

docs.title: Afterword
docs.text: I didn't expect myself to go slightly deeper into the SSL/TLS handshake territory. After reading the blog posts from Cloudflare and back-and-forth questions with Claude, I finally gain a tiny bit understanding of the handshake that ensures the security and privacy of the communication between the client and the server.

docs.title: Five CI/CD Failures Deploying to a VPS as a Non-Root User
docs.text:
A GitHub Actions deploy to a VPS that broke one step at a time when the pipeline moved from root to a dedicated deploy user — and how each failure was diagnosed and fixed:

  • git pull failing with the error "Host key verification failed" (no known_hosts, no deploy key)
  • git remote get-url origin still pointing at a fork
  • systemctl restart demanding the root password because the sudoers rule was never invoked
  • a package-lock.json accidentally gitignored, and
  • a .venv whose bin/python symlink pointed into /root.

This blog post also contains the original deploy.yml file that has the above issues, and the golftracker.service for readers in the future who might need an example of a .service file.

docs.title: Deploy YAML code
docs.text:
Below is the initial code for the problematic CI/CD workflow (deploy.yml).

name: Balling.au CI/CD Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Deploy to Production
        uses: appleboy/ssh-action@v1.2.0
        with:
          host: ${{ secrets.VPS_HOST }}
          username: ${{ secrets.VPS_USER }}
          key: ${{ secrets.SSH_PRIVATE_KEY }}
          script_stop: true
          script: |
            cd /var/www/golf-score-tracker

            echo "--- Pulling latest code ---"
            git pull origin main
            echo "--- Syncing Python dependencies & running migrations ---"
            /home/deploy/.local/bin/uv sync
            PYTHONPATH=/var/www/golf-score-tracker/backend /home/deploy/.local/bin/uv run alembic upgrade head

            echo "--- Building Frontend ---"
            cd frontend
            # Use sed to safely replace or append the VITE_API_URL without wiping .env
            if grep -q "^VITE_API_URL=" .env; then
              sed -i 's|^VITE_API_URL=.*|VITE_API_URL=${{ secrets.VITE_API_URL }}|' .env
            else
              echo "VITE_API_URL=${{ secrets.VITE_API_URL }}" >> .env
            fi
            npm install
            npm run build

            echo "--- Restarting Service ---"
            cd ..
            systemctl restart golftracker
            echo "Deployment completed successfully."

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
When transitioning the CI/CD workflow from the root user to a dedicated deploy user, I encountered the following error during the git pull step:

YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.SSSSSSSZ --- Pulling latest code ---
YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.SSSSSSSZ Host key verification failed.
YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.SSSSSSSZ fatal: Could not read from remote repository.
YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.SSSSSSSZ Please make sure you have the correct access rights
YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.SSSSSSSZ and the repository exists.
YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.SSSSSSSZ 2026/09/22 14:29:19 Process exited with status 1
YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.SSSSSSSZ ##[error]Process completed with exit code 1.

This error message is from line 23 git pull origin main.

docs.title: Why It Happened
docs.text:
When the git pull command was executed, the SSH client attempted to verify the server's identity. Because this is an automated CI/CD workflow, there was no human available to respond to the interactive prompt: "Are you sure you want to continue connecting?". ssh aborted and presented the error: Host key verification failed.

The fundamental issue is that the deploy user had not completed the two-way authentication required for secure communication.

  • /home/deploy/.ssh/known_hosts was missing (No Host Trust).
  • /home/deploy/.ssh/id_ed25519 and its public counterpart (.pub) were missing (No User Authentication).

Note: While /home/deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys existed, it only allowed GitHub to SSH into the VPS. It did not help the VPS talk to GitHub.

To understand why the fix required both ssh-keyscan and a new keypair, we can look at the SSH handshake between the Client (VPS) and the Server (GitHub):

  1. TCP Connection: A connection is established.
  2. Server Identity Check (Host Trust): The server presents its host key. The client (the VPS) checks its known_hosts file to see if it recognises the server. (This is where the failure occurred).
  3. Client Identity Check (User Authentication): The server (GitHub) checks its authorized_keys (or Deploy Keys) to see if the user is authorised. For this to work, GitHub uses the VPS' public key to verify the signature, proving the VPS owns the private key. Nothing is encrypted to the client key.
  4. Encrypted Session: A secure session is established, and the git command is executed. When the git pull origin main command is executed, data is encrypted under the symmetric session key from the key exchange (Diffie‑Hellman). The host key authenticates the server; the client key authenticates the client. Neither one carries the payload.

The authorized_keys file and the known_hosts file belong to different "directions".

  1. Inbound: GitHub \(\rightarrow\) VPS (The "Guest List")

    When your GitHub Action runs, the Runner is the Client and your VPS is the Server.

    • The Goal: The VPS needs to know the Runner is allowed to enter.
    • The Tool: The VPS uses authorized_keys as a Guest List. If the Runner's key is on that list, the VPS lets them in.
    • This is why your Runner could SSH into the VPS successfully.

  2. Outbound: VPS \(\rightarrow\) GitHub (The "Contact List")

    When your git pull command runs, your VPS is now the Client and GitHub is the Server.

    • The Goal: The VPS needs to know it is actually talking to the real GitHub and not a malicious imposter (a Man-in-the-Middle attack).
    • The Tool: The VPS uses known_hosts as a Contact List. It looks up GitHub's "fingerprint" in that file to ensure the server is legitimate.
    • This is where you failed: the VPS had no "Contact List" for GitHub, so it couldn't "recognise" it.

Below is the SSH file reference guide.

File Purpose Direction authorized_keys Lists clients/servers authorised to log in. Inbound (e.g., GitHub \(\rightarrow\) VPS) known_hosts Stores identities of trusted servers. Outbound (e.g., VPS \(\rightarrow\) GitHub) id_ed25519 The private key used to prove identity. Outbound (e.g., VPS \(\rightarrow\) GitHub) id_ed25519.pub The public key shared with the server. Outbound (e.g., VPS \(\rightarrow\) GitHub)

docs.title: The Solution
docs.text:
1. Log in as deploy user: ssh deploy@[ip-address]
  2. Confirm the user: whoami
  3. Generate a fresh key-pair value: ssh-keygen -t ed25519
    • The system will prompt for a file path to save the key: 
      Generating public/private ed25519 key pair.
Enter file in which to save the key (/home/deploy/.ssh/id_ed25519):
      Press Enter to save the key pair in the default location.
    • Next, it will prompt for a passphrase: 
      Enter passphrase (empty for no passphrase):
      Press Enter to use an empty passphrase (required for unattended CI/CD).
    • It will prompt you to confirm the empty passphrase: 
      Enter same passphrase again:
      Press Enter again.
    • The output will display the results: 
      Your identification has been saved in /home/deploy/.ssh/id_ed25519
Your public key has been saved in /home/deploy/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
The key fingerprint is:
SHA256:...
The key's randomart image is:
+--[ED25519 256]--+
| ...             |
| ...             |
+----[SHA256]-----+

  4. Ensure correct permissions

    • chmod 700 /home/deploy/.ssh
    • chmod 600 /home/deploy/.ssh/id_ed25519
    • chmod 644 /home/deploy/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

    Info

    Note: Understanding Permissions

    • chmod 700: Owner has Read, Write, and Execute permissions (7 = 4+2+1); Group and Others have none.
    • chmod 600: Owner has Read and Write permissions (6 = 4+2); Group and Others have none.
    • chmod 644: Owner has Read and Write; Group and Others have Read-only access.

  5. Retrieve the public key: cat /home/deploy/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

    • The .pub file contains your public key.
    • Example content: ssh-ed25519 AAAA... deploy@Balling

  6. Register the key on GitHub:

    • Go to Repository > Settings > Deploy keys > Add deploy key.
    • Title: deploy@Balling
    • Key: Paste the content from step 5.
    • Allow write access: Leave this unchecked (the production server only needs to pull code, not push).

  7. Trust the GitHub host:

    • Run the following commands 
      ssh-keyscan -t ed25519 github.com >> ~/.ssh/known_hosts
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/known_hosts
cat ~/.ssh/known_hosts
    • Security Tip: Verify that the fingerprint in your known_hosts matches the official fingerprints listed in the GitHub Documentation.

  8. Verify: ssh -T git@github.com

    • You should see a greeting message from GitHub (e.g., "Hi username/repository! You've successfully authenticated...").

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
During the deployment process, I discovered that the local repository on the VPS was tracking the wrong remote. Running git remote -v revealed that the origin was pointing to a fork rather than my own canonical repository.

origin  git@github.com:Collaborator/repository.git (fetch)
origin  git@github.com:Collaborator/repository.git (push)

This meant that any new code pushed to my repository (reynardo-tjhin/repository) would not be picked up by the CI/CD pipeline, as the server was still pulling from the fork.

docs.title: Why It Happened
docs.text: This was a configuration oversight during the initial setup. A collaborator had been tasked with setting up the CI/CD workflow and, to test the process safely, had performed the initial configuration using their own fork of the project. Consequently, the VPS was configured to track the fork instead of the primary repository.

docs.title: The Solution
docs.text:
The fix involved repointing the origin remote to my repository and verifying that the connection was correctly established.

  1. Repoint the Remote URL

    I updated the remote URL to point to the correct repository. It is important to use the SSH format (git@github.com:...) rather than HTTPS, as the deploy user relies on SSH Deploy Keys for authentication.

    git remote set-url origin git@github.com:reynardo-tjhin/repository.git

  2. Verify the Change

    I confirmed the update by checking the remote configuration again: git remote -v Expected output: 

    origin  git@github.com:reynardo-tjhin/repository.git (fetch)
origin  git@github.com:reynardo-tjhin/repository.git (push)

  3. Ensure a Clean Transition (Best Practice)

    Before running the first deployment, I performed a "dry-run" fetch to ensure there were no divergence issues between the fork and the main repository:

    # Fetch the latest state from the new origin
git fetch origin

# Check the status to ensure a clean fast-forward is possible
git status -sb

    Note: If the repositories had diverged, I would have needed to perform a git reset --hard origin/main to align the VPS strictly with the canonical repository.

docs.title: Issue #3: systemctl restart Asks for the Root Password
Problem
docs.text: Line 41 systemctl restart golftracker stops the CI/CD script and causes a new issue: "Authentication is required to restart 'golftracker.service' Authenticating as: root Password: ".

docs.title: Why It Happened
docs.text:
There are two doors to a privileged systemctl verb, and only one of them had been configured on this VPS:

  • polkit/systemd — for a remote SSH session, its default is to demand the root password. That is why the prompt read Authenticating as: root and not [sudo] password for deploy.
  • sudo — requires a matching rule in sudoers, and is consulted only when you actually type sudo.

Why polkit is involved at all: a system unit belongs to the system manager (PID 1), and systemctl does not act on files — it sends a D-Bus message to PID 1 saying "restart this unit". PID 1 then asks polkit whether the caller may manage system units, and for a remote SSH session the answer defaults to "only with admin authentication". That gate sits in front of the unit, so it applies whatever the unit's own User= says.

When my collaborator moved the pipeline from root to a dedicated deploy user, he had already gone through the second door and added the rule for it:

$ sudo -l -U deploy
User deploy may run the following commands on Balling:
    (ALL) NOPASSWD: /bin/systemctl restart golftracker

So deploy was allowed to restart the service. The step still failed because line 41 ran bare systemctl restart golftracker — no sudo, so sudoers was never read. The command fell through to polkit instead, polkit asked for the root password, and in CI there is nobody to type it. The permission existed; the workflow simply never asked for it.

For reference, an unprivileged user can run read-only verbs such as systemctl status golftracker or systemctl list-units without any privilege. restart on a system unit — and this one runs as User=root (line 6 of the unit file below) — is always refused with Permission denied / Authentication required / must be root.

The below shows the content of /etc/systemd/system/golftracker.service.

[Unit]
Description=Golf Score Tracker API
After=network.target

[Service]
User=root
WorkingDirectory=/var/www/golf-score-tracker
Environment="PYTHONPATH=/var/www/golf-score-tracker/backend"
EnvironmentFile=/var/www/golf-score-tracker/.env
ExecStart=/var/www/golf-score-tracker/.venv/bin/gunicorn app.main:app -w 4 -k uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker --bind 0.0.0.0:8000
Restart=always

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Info

User=root describes which account the process runs as once systemd has started it. It has no bearing on who may restart the unit — that decision is made before systemd looks at the setting.

docs.title: The Solution
docs.text:
Tip: run sudo -iu deploy to become the deploy user.

  1. SSH into the VPS as the root user.

  2. Check the user deploy's permission.

    • run sudo -l -U deploy.
    • if the (ALL) NOPASSWD: /bin/systemctl restart golftracker line is already present, skip to step 5 — the server was already authorised and only the workflow was wrong.
    • if instead it ends with User deploy is not allowed to run sudo on Balling, continue to step 3.

  3. Grant the deploy user permission to run this one command without a password.

    • as the root user, create a file deploy in /etc/sudoers.d: sudo EDITOR=nano visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/deploy
    • write the following content to the file: deploy ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /bin/systemctl restart golftracker
    • save the file: CTRL + X > y > ENTER

    Info

    visudo edits the file the same way nano does, but refuses to save if the syntax does not parse and restores mode 440. A sudoers error that nano would happily save breaks sudo for every account on the machine. Note also that drop-in filenames may not contain a . — deploy.bak in that directory is silently ignored.

  4. Check the user deploy's permission again.

    • run sudo -l -U deploy: we should see the following. 
      Matching Defaults entries for deploy on Balling:
    env_reset, mail_badpass, secure_path=/usr/local/sbin\:/usr/local/bin\:/usr/sbin\:/usr/bin\:/sbin\:/bin\:/snap/bin, use_pty

User deploy may run the following commands on Balling:
    (ALL) NOPASSWD: /bin/systemctl restart golftracker
    • run sudo -iu deploy to become the deploy user — sudoers does not apply to root, so the command has to be run as deploy to prove the rule works
    • run sudo -n /bin/systemctl restart golftracker; echo $?: we should see 0
    • run exit to leave the deploy user

  5. In the deploy.yml file, change systemctl restart golftracker to sudo -n /bin/systemctl restart golftracker. -n matters for CI: non-interactive — fail fast instead of hanging on [sudo] password for deploy: prompt that nobody can answer in Actions.

Info

sudoers matches the command literally. sudo -n /bin/systemctl restart golftracker.service fails with sudo: a password is required even though systemd accepts both spellings, because golftracker and golftracker.service are different strings. Keep the rule and the workflow character-for-character identical.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: While tidying the project, I accidentally added package-lock.json to .gitignore — the kind of small mistake that is easy to make and easy to miss. On its own, nothing breaks, but it hurts as soon as you work with more developers or deploy to a server: without the lockfile, npm install can resolve different dependency versions on each machine. If those resolutions land on different major versions of a library, the code that works on one machine may not work on another — including the production server. This issue would never have happened if the lockfile had simply stayed tracked.

docs.title: The Solution
docs.text:
All commands below run inside frontend/ unless stated otherwise: the lockfile always sits next to the package.json it describes, so the file this issue is about is frontend/package-lock.json.

  1. Remove the package-lock.json entry from .gitignore (the lockfile itself should be tracked). Check both the root .gitignore and frontend/.gitignore — the rule can hide in either.
  2. Get the latest working package-lock.json (I took it from my collaborator's commit since he was the one that initialised the packages for the frontend.)
  3. Run npm ci (not npm install)
    • npm install is only run once to install the packages and generate the package-lock.json.
    • Because I recovered the lockfile from an older commit, npm ci doubles as a check: it only succeeds if package-lock.json and package.json are still in sync. If they had drifted apart, it fails right here, on my machine, instead of silently breaking the production deploy.
  4. Update the deploy.yml (don't run both npm install and npm ci; change npm install to npm ci).
  5. Commit the package-lock.json and deploy.yml to the repository.

Info

Why running both npm install and npm ci is incorrect:

  • npm install re-resolves the caret (^) ranges in package.json on every run and can rewrite package-lock.json on the server — and that modified lockfile is never committed back, so the server quietly drifts away from everyone else's versions.
  • Running npm ci immediately after deletes node_modules/ and reinstalls everything from the lockfile anyway — so the preceding npm install only costs time and reintroduces non-determinism for zero benefit. Replace the npm install step with npm ci; don't append.
  • Also note that npm ci cannot work without a lockfile: if package-lock.json is not committed, it fails on the VPS with a "missing lockfile" error. That is why both changes must ship together — the lockfile committed, and the workflow switched to npm ci only.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
With the deploy user finally able to run the workflow, the next step produced a new error. The failing line was /home/deploy/.local/bin/uv sync:

YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.SSSSSSSZ error: Failed to query Python interpreter
YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.SSSSSSSZ   cause: failed to canonicalize path `/var/www/golf-score-tracker/.venv/bin/python`: Permission denied (os error 13)

At first glance this looks like deploy cannot read the virtual environment — but deploy owned the .venv and could read every file in it. So what was blocked?

docs.title: Why It Happened
docs.text:
This was the last leftover from the root → deploy migration. A virtual environment does not contain its own Python interpreter - it symlinks bin/python to the real interpreter somewhere else. uv keeps its own Python installations under ~/.local/share/uv/python/, and the venv had been built back when uv sync ran as root, where ~ is /root. So .venv/bin/python pointed at /root/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.13-.../bin/python3.13.

To find exactly where deploy got blocked, I walked the path with namei -l. It prints the permissions and owner of every component from / to the target, follows the final symlink, and walks the target's path too:

$ namei -l /var/www/golf-score-tracker/.venv/bin/python

# ... (components up to .venv/bin resolve fine) ...

lrwxrwxrwx deploy deploy python -> /root/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.13-linux-x86_64-gnu/bin/python3.13
drwxr-xr-x root root /
drwx------ root root root
                   .local - Permission denied

The last three lines are the whole diagnosis: /root is drwx------ (700), so deploy cannot even enter it — let alone reach the interpreter inside. To "canonicalise" a path, uv must traverse every directory along it, which fails at /root with Permission denied (os error 13).

I checked the symlink itself first (command: stat -c '%U %G %a' /var/www/golf-score-tracker/.venv/bin/python*) and it showed 777 permissions — a red herring. Symlinks always show rwxrwxrwx, and Linux ignores symlink permissions entirely; access is decided by each directory traversed along the way. That is why a 777 link can still be unreachable: deploy was stopped at /root, before the link's target was ever reached.

docs.title: The Solution
docs.text:
Info

Where does uv know the virtual environment is in .venv? Nowhere in the repo - I have no [tool.uv] section and no uv.toml. It is uv's default convention: it walks up from the current directory to find pyproject.toml, then uses <project-root>/.venv. That is also why the sync command must run from the project root - run it from frontend/ or backend/ and uv would create a second venv somewhere else.

  1. Confirm the diagnosis: readlink /var/www/golf-score-tracker/.venv/bin/python: if it prints a path under /root/, the venv is bound to root's interpreter.
  2. Give deploy its own interpreter (as deploy): uv python install 3.13 - the version pin comes from .python-version in the repository. This downloads CPython into /home/deploy/.local/share/uv/python/.... Doing this before deleting anything keeps the downtime window short: uv sync below then reuses the installed interpreter instead of downloading it mid-deploy.
  3. Stop the service (as root): systemctl stop golftracker.
  4. Delete the root-bound .venv folder (as root): rm -rf /var/www/golf-score-tracker/.venv. No backup is needed - uv.lock + pyproject.toml + .python-version fully determine the environment, so a fresh uv sync rebuilds it.
  5. Recreate it as deploy from the project root: cd /var/www/golf-score-tracker && uv sync — builds a fresh .venv deploy-owned end-to-end, with bin/python pointing inside /home/deploy/....
  6. Bring everything back up: uv run alembic upgrade head, the frontend build (Issue #4's npm ci), then sudo -n /bin/systemctl restart golftracker. The first two are optional - the next CI run repeats them - but the restart is not: step 3 left the service stopped.

Verify:

  • readlink .venv/bin/python: a /home/deploy/... path, no /root anywhere.
  • ls -ld on the .venv shows deploy deploy ownership.
  • uv sync runs clean - no "canonicalize ... Permission denied".
